Circle In Isosceles Triangle

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: Move the corners of an isosceles triangle and the two points on its sides, and watch the circle follow them.
How to play: Drag A, B, C, P or Q with a mouse or finger, or focus a point and use the arrow keys. Press Check the claim to test what you see.
Look for the math

Here is a small surprise. Pick two points on the equal sides of an isosceles triangle so that the short pieces from the top and the far base corner match. Draw the circle through the top and those two points. It always goes through one fixed point of the triangle, even as you drag everything around.

The setup

In an isosceles triangle ABC, the sides AB and AC are equal. P sits on AB and Q sits on AC, and neither is a corner. The rule is AP = CQ. The circle you see is the circumcircle of APQ, and the green dot is O, the center of the circle through A, B and C.

Equal power gives OP = OQ

Because AB = AC and AP = CQ, the leftover pieces are equal too: PB = QA. So PA·PB = QC·QA. These two products are the power of P and Q with respect to the big circle. Writing the power as R² − OP², with R the circumradius, gives R² − OP² = R² − OQ², hence OP = OQ.

Equal angles put O on the circle

The line AO cuts the top angle in half. Using the sine rule in triangles AOP and AOQ with AO common and OP = OQ gives sin∠APO = sin∠AQO. Unless P and Q are the midpoints, those angles are not equal, so they add to 180 degrees. Four points with opposite angles like that form a cyclic quadrilateral: A, P, O and Q lie on one circle. The midpoint case is the symmetric case where the quadrilateral is an isosceles trapezoid, and it works too.

What the logic test checks

The core keeps one number t, placing P at t·A + (1−t)·B and Q at t·C + (1−t)·A. On 500 shapes it checks AP = CQ, PA·PB = QC·QA, OP = OQ, ∠POQ = 2∠ACB (so ∠BAC + ∠POQ = 180°), and the real cross ratio from the article's complex-number proof. The centers and circle match a second transcription of the applet's own bytecode: midpoint perpendiculars intersected to find O, and the mean of the three distances for the drawn radius. One small deviation: the applet's code for dragging corner B overwrites C.y twice, breaking the isosceles shape, so this page mirrors C across the axis as it does when corner C is dragged; that keeps the triangle isosceles as the problem needs.

Try a very tall, narrow triangle, then a very flat one, and press Check the claim each time. Try dragging P almost to B and watch Q move with it.
